units.title: 高一专项：观鸟笔记与长椅修复

materials.title: Field Notes And Bench · Reading
materials.text:
On my first birdwatching walk, I wanted my notebook to look like the guide's. Hers contained neat names beside the times of sightings. Mine began with a drawing of a grey shape I could not identify. ____1____ I thought an unfinished description was less useful than a correct name.

The guide asked me to add where the bird had been and what it was doing. I wrote that it had moved along the water's edge and stopped beside a red post. ____2____ She explained that those details might help us understand the sighting later, even if the species remained uncertain.

Further along the path, I heard a call and immediately wrote down the name of a bird I knew from a recording. The guide asked whether I had seen it. ____3____ I changed my note to say that I had heard a similar call, leaving the identification open.

At the end of the walk, we compared our pages. Her notebook included a question mark beside one sighting. ____4____ It marked a point she wanted to investigate rather than a mistake she hoped nobody would notice.

I went home with fewer names than I had expected, but with a more useful record of the morning. ____5____ Next time, I would leave room for what I had observed and what I still needed to find out.

options: Even an experienced observer could leave a question unanswered.

The blank spaces no longer seemed like evidence that I had failed.
The description was becoming a record rather than an empty space.
A familiar recording proved that every similar sound came from the same species.
I had only heard a sound from beyond the reeds.

materials.title: Field Notes And Bench · Grammar
materials.text:
Last week, the council invited our class to help choose the wording for a sign beside a repaired park bench. The bench ____1____ (DAMAGE) during a storm in the winter, and a local carpenter had restored it. We wanted the sign ____2____ (EXPLAIN) what had happened without becoming too long.

The carpenter, ____3____ came to talk to us, showed a photograph of the broken seat. He said that some old pieces could still ____4____ (USE), while others had to be replaced. We had assumed that repair always meant keeping every original part.

One pupil wrote a sentence thanking the people ____5____ had helped. Another suggested adding the month of the repair. The teacher asked us to read both sentences ____6____ (LOUD) and decide whether the information was clear.

Our first draft was longer ____7____ the space available on the sign. After ____8____ (DISCUSS) what mattered most, we shortened the description but kept the date and the carpenter's name.

On Friday, we saw the finished sign beside the bench. It reminded ____9____ (WE) that a familiar object could have a history worth noticing. We were pleased ____10____ (SEE) people stopping to read it before sitting down.

units.title: 高一专项：共享午餐与花园诗会

materials.title: Shared Lunch And Garden · Reading
materials.text:
Our class planned a shared lunch in which each group would prepare one dish. At first, we wrote a list of dish names and thought the plan was complete. Then one student asked what was actually in each dish. ____1____ A name such as “vegetable pie” did not identify every ingredient.

We asked groups to keep a written ingredient list beside their food. If someone changed the recipe, the list needed to change too. ____2____ A label copied from an earlier plan would not describe the dish that people were about to eat.

Serving arrangements mattered as well. Two dishes could be clearly labelled and still become mixed if everyone used the same spoon. ____3____ We placed a separate serving utensil beside each container and asked volunteers to check the arrangement.

The teacher also reminded us that nobody had to explain a personal reason for choosing one dish rather than another. ____4____ A student could ask about an ingredient or bring their own food without turning lunch into a public discussion of private information.

Afterwards, we kept notes about what had been difficult to organise. ____5____ The next class would need more than a photograph of smiling people to understand why the lunch had worked as well as it did.

options: An unchanged label was correct even when the recipe changed completely.

Every student had to announce a private reason before taking any food.
The information had to follow the food rather than the original intention.
Providing information was different from demanding an explanation.

materials.title: Shared Lunch And Garden · Grammar
materials.text:
Our school held a poetry afternoon in an old walled garden. Before the event, a gardener ____1____ (SHOW) us which paths visitors could use. A section near the wall was closed ____2____ repairs, so we moved the chairs to the open lawn.

The student ____3____ had designed the programme was worried about the change. Her original plan placed each reader beneath a different tree. The gardener helped us find a ____4____ (SIMPLE) arrangement that left the paths clear.

While two students ____5____ (CARRY) the chairs, the rest of us put numbers on the seats. We avoided ____6____ (FIX) anything to the old trees. Small cards on stands were easy to move and did not damage the bark.

The audience arrived ____7____ (EARLY) than we expected. We asked them ____8____ (WAIT) near the gate until the final sound check was finished. The gardener stayed with us and answered questions about the plants.

At the end, all the cards ____9____ (COLLECT) before the chairs were stacked away. The garden looked much as it had that morning, but ____10____ (WE) notes contained several ideas for a future event.

materials.title: Trial Board And Piano · Reading
materials.text:
Our science club's first exhibition board showed a photograph of three thriving plants and the heading “The Best Soil”. We were proud of the result until a visitor asked how we had reached that conclusion. ____1____ The photograph showed an outcome, but it did not explain the comparison.

We added a description of the containers, light and watering schedule. We also wrote down how long the plants had grown. ____2____ Without those details, another class could not tell which conditions we had kept the same.

One plant had been moved away from the window for a day when the room was cleaned. We nearly left that incident out because it made the method look untidy. ____3____ A reader might reasonably want to know about an unplanned difference in light.

We also changed the heading. Instead of naming a universally best soil, we described what had happened in our particular trial. ____4____ We had tested a small number of plants under one set of conditions, not every plant in every garden.

The revised board was less dramatic but easier to discuss. ____5____ Visitors began asking how we might repeat the trial rather than simply praising the green leaves in the photograph.

These were parts of the experiment that a picture could not supply.
A successful photograph proved that no method needed to be recorded.
However, hiding it would make the account less useful.

materials.title: Trial Board And Piano · Grammar
materials.text:
A community centre asked our music club to record the sound of its old piano. The instrument ____1____ (REPAIR) earlier that year, and the staff wanted a short recording for the centre's website. Our teacher reminded us ____2____ (ASK) permission before recording anyone's voice.

We chose a time ____3____ the building was usually quiet. However, a delivery arrived just as the first piece began. The pianist stopped and waited ____4____ (PATIENT) while boxes were carried through the hall.

On the second attempt, the sound was ____5____ (CLEAR) than before. We had moved the microphone away from a noisy fan. A volunteer ____6____ was listening through headphones pointed out a chair scraping in the background.

Instead of ____7____ (IGNORE) the noise, we moved the chair and tried again. We kept a note of the changes so that we could understand why one version sounded different ____8____ another.

The final file ____9____ (SEND) to the pianist for approval before it went online. She was pleased with it, and we learned that making a simple recording could involve many ____10____ (DECIDE).

units.title: 高二专项：舞伴线索与旧桥照片

materials.title: Dance Cues And Footbridge · Reading
materials.text:
When I joined a community dance class, I tried to remember every movement as a word. Left, turn, pause, step back: I repeated the list silently while the instructor demonstrated. ____1____ By the time I had named one action, the group had often moved on to the next.

The instructor suggested watching the direction of my partner's shoulders instead of staring at my own feet. ____2____ The turn began to feel connected to another person rather than to an instruction I had to retrieve alone.

This did not mean abandoning the sequence. Between attempts, I still asked about the part I had missed. ____3____ Knowing which moment caused trouble allowed the instructor to demonstrate a short section rather than repeat everything from the beginning.

One evening, a different partner made a small mistake and stopped. I recognised the look of frustration and offered to start again. ____4____ Until then, I had imagined that only the experienced members contributed anything to the class.

I never became the quickest learner in the room. What changed was how I measured a useful evening. ____5____ A clearer response to a partner or a better question about one transition could matter as much as getting through the whole dance without a pause.

That gave me a cue already built into the movement.
Helping someone restart changed my sense of my own place in the group.

materials.title: Dance Cues And Footbridge · Grammar
materials.text:
A photograph of the old footbridge had been displayed in our school corridor for years before anyone questioned its date. The label said 1938, but a local resident remembered the bridge ____1____ (BUILD) after the war. Our history group decided ____2____ (INVESTIGATE) the difference.

The photographer's name, ____3____ appeared faintly on the back, led us to a collection of his work. There we found another image taken from almost the same position. A notice in the background was ____4____ (EASY) to read than the handwriting on our print.

It advertised a fair held in 1952. That did not prove the exact day on ____5____ the photograph had been taken, but it made the old label doubtful. We asked the archivist whether the date might refer to an earlier bridge rather ____6____ the structure in the picture.

After ____7____ (COMPARE) the surrounding buildings, she agreed that this was possible. She advised us not to replace one uncertain date ____8____ another without explaining the evidence.

Our new caption described the problem instead of hiding it. The photograph ____9____ (MOVE) to a clearer display case, and visitors were invited to share any further information. Within a week, a retired builder contacted ____10____ (WE) with a copy of a later survey.

units.title: 高二专项：读书会分歧与临时站牌

materials.title: Reading Circle And Bus Stop · Reading
materials.text:
Our reading circle nearly rejected a short story because several members disliked its ending. Others wanted to discuss it precisely because it had unsettled them. Before voting, we realised that we were answering different questions. ____1____ Enjoying a story immediately was not the same as finding it worth examining together.

We decided to give everyone a short turn to identify one passage they wanted to revisit. ____2____ Someone who disliked the ending could point to the moment that had created an expectation, while someone who admired it could explain what changed on a second reading.

The discussion also needed room for members who had not reached the final page. We agreed to announce clearly before discussing the ending. ____3____ Those members could then choose whether to stay for that part rather than discover the outcome by accident.

One participant brought a review from a newspaper. It offered an interesting interpretation, but the group did not treat it as a final answer. ____4____ We compared its claims with particular sentences in the story instead of using the critic's name to settle our disagreement.

By the end, we had not reached a shared judgement of the ending. We had, however, become more precise about our differences. ____5____ The next meeting began with a better question than a simple request to say whether the book was good.

Agreement was not the only possible sign of a productive discussion.
A specific passage gave each opinion something that others could examine.
The newspaper review automatically made every other interpretation invalid.
That warning allowed people to make an informed choice about listening.

At our school's fabric exchange, a folded piece of cloth could look large enough for a project and still be unsuitable. One student discovered a narrow strip cut from the centre only after taking a piece home. ____1____ A neat outer rectangle did not guarantee that the whole area could be used.

The club also separated a known fibre label from a guess based on touch. ____3____ If no original label survived, the card said that the composition was uncertain rather than presenting someone's impression as a fact.

Small samples raised a different issue. They were useful for patching, testing a stitch or making a badge, even when too small for a bag. ____4____ We created a separate box for those pieces instead of treating size as a simple measure of value.

At the end, the exchange had fewer impressive stacks but more usable information. ____5____ People could choose material for a particular purpose without assuming that every folded piece was a complete, identical kind of thing.

materials.text:
Before a long walking holiday, I bought a notebook with enough pages for one careful account of every day. I expected it to become a record of places reached. On the second afternoon, heavy rain forced us to stop short of the village where we had planned to sleep. ____1____ I stared at the small distance on the map and felt that I had little worth writing down.

The evening itself did not support that judgement. The owner of a roadside guesthouse lent us dry clothes while ours hung by a heater. Another walker showed me how to repair a loose strap. ____2____ My notebook's idea of a successful day was narrower than the experience I was actually having.

I began writing about those exchanges, but I worried that this would turn an account of a walking journey into something less serious. A friend asked why the planned route should have exclusive authority over the story. ____3____ The question made me notice how much of my disappointment came from comparing events with an outline written before the journey began.

The remaining pages became less uniform. Some contained distances; others preserved a conversation or a question about a place we had passed without stopping. ____4____ I had not stopped caring where we walked. I had stopped requiring every meaningful part of the trip to look like progress along a line.

Months later, those uneven pages were what brought the holiday back. ____5____ The unfinished route and the unexpected evening belonged to the same journey, rather than one being an excuse for the other.

materials.text:
When our mural was photographed for the local paper, the caption named only the student who had drawn the original design. She was surprised, because the wall had taken a dozen people several weekends to complete. ____1____ The published name was accurate in one sense while leaving most of the work invisible.

The group first considered replacing it with a list of every participant. That would improve recognition, but it would not explain the different contributions. ____2____ Preparing the surface, adjusting colours and organising access had each shaped what could finally be painted.

At our next meeting, the designer described how the image itself had changed through discussion. A classmate's suggestion had altered the position of the central figure; another person's experience had made a planned detail seem inappropriate. ____3____ The design was not a fixed object that everyone else had merely transferred to a wall.

This did not mean that individual work should disappear into a vague claim that “the community” had done everything. ____4____ We needed an account that could acknowledge particular decisions without making one person's contribution stand for the whole process.

The revised caption was short, followed by a link to a fuller project record. It named the initial designer and described the work as a collaboration. ____5____ It gave readers a more honest starting point and gave us a reason to preserve the account of how the wall had changed.

My aunt's recipe notebook was full of instructions that seemed incomplete to me. “A little more if the day is cold,” one margin said, without explaining more of what. I decided to type the recipes into a document so that the family could use them. ____1____ I imagined replacing every uncertainty with a precise number.

Working beside my aunt changed the task. She did not always use the quantity that she had written years earlier. She looked at the ingredients and adjusted her method. ____2____ The notebook was a reminder for someone with experience, not a complete course for a stranger.

I still wanted the typed version to help relatives who had never watched her cook. Rather than silently filling the gaps, I asked questions and marked which explanations came from our new conversation. ____3____ Readers could then distinguish an old note from a later attempt to explain it.

Some details resisted a simple rule. The same instruction could refer to a texture rather than to a fixed time. I added descriptions of what my aunt was looking for and kept her warning that experience would still matter. ____4____ A document could support learning without pretending to replace every judgement made in the kitchen.

When the pages were finished, my aunt asked me to keep a scan of the original beside them. ____5____ The two versions served different readers, and preserving both made their relationship clearer than declaring either one the final, perfect recipe book.

materials.title: Recipe History And Seating Plan · Grammar
materials.text:
Hardly ____1____ (WE/OPEN) the theatre's old seating plan when we noticed that several rows had been drawn in pencil over the printed arrangement. The plan ____2____ (KEEP) with papers from a single season, but the additions appeared to record changes made later.

The archivist, ____3____ advice we trusted, asked us to examine the annotations before assigning them a date. One note described a wider aisle, while another referred to a door ____4____ was no longer visible in recent photographs. Neither detail alone established when the alteration had taken place.

____5____ interested us was that the pencil lines did not simply add more seats. In one area, they reduced the number. The archivist suggested that a practical change might have required ____6____ (REMOVE) a row rather than maximising capacity.

We compared the sheet with a later programme. A seating diagram in that booklet made the altered entrance easier ____7____ (IDENTIFY). Even so, we could not be certain ____8____ the pencilled plan had been used for an actual performance or remained a proposal.

Had we assumed that every mark represented completed work, we ____9____ (OVERSTATE) the evidence. Our final description therefore distinguished the printed plan, the added lines and the remaining ____10____ (CERTAIN) about their use.

questions.explanation: Hardly前置过去完成倒装had we opened，did后不可过去分词opened。
plan单数被保存，过去或过去完成被动。
whose advice表所属。
door作从句主语which/that。
What主语从句中作interested主语。
require doing或require the removal of a row均可；to removing混接，removed缺be。
easier to identify形容词后不定式。
是否实际用或仅提案，whether/if引导二选问题。

questions.prompt: Gap 9 (OVERSTATE): Describe an unreal result in the past. Use 1 to 3 words.
